power-management-001.question: In the CMOS dynamic power formula P = αCV²f, what does α represent?
choices: The number of transistors
The fraction of signals switching per clock cycle (the activity factor)
The chip temperature
power-management-001.explanation: Dynamic power is consumed charging and discharging the capacitance of wires and gates. C is the switched capacitance, V the supply voltage, f the clock frequency and α the activity factor, the fraction of signals that switch per clock. Parts whose data does not change, or whose clocks are stopped, do not switch, so reducing α is also an important power-saving lever.
choiceNotes: Transistor count is folded into the capacitance C.
Correct. Circuits that do not switch use no dynamic power.
Temperature mainly affects static power.

power-management-002.question: What is the dynamic power of a circuit with activity factor α = 0.1, switched capacitance C = 1 nF, supply voltage V = 1 V and frequency f = 1 GHz?
choices: 1 W
power-management-002.explanation: Substituting into P = αCV²f gives 0.1 × 1 × 10⁻⁹ F × (1 V)² × 1 × 10⁹ Hz = 0.1 W. The nano (10⁻⁹) of the capacitance and the giga (10⁹) of the frequency cancel, which keeps the arithmetic simple. In real chips the switched capacitance grows with circuit size, and total dynamic power can reach tens to hundreds of watts.
choiceNotes: That forgets to multiply by α.
The order of magnitude is wrong.

power-management-003.question: With the supply voltage unchanged, only the clock frequency is halved. What happens to the dynamic energy needed to finish a fixed amount of computation?
choices: It stays about the same (power halves but time doubles)
It halves
It falls to a quarter
power-management-003.explanation: Dynamic power is proportional to f, so halving the frequency halves the power. But the same computation takes twice as long, so energy, power times time, is unchanged, because the energy per switching event is set by CV². Reducing energy requires lowering voltage; lowering frequency is what allows the circuit to work correctly at that lower voltage.
choiceNotes: Correct. Energy = power × time.
Power halves, but time doubles.
Without lowering voltage it does not fall that far.

power-management-004.question: Assume DVFS can lower the supply voltage in proportion to frequency. When frequency is halved, roughly what happens to dynamic power and to the dynamic energy for a fixed amount of computation?
choices: Power falls to one-eighth and energy to one-quarter
Both power and energy halve
Power falls to a quarter and energy is unchanged
power-management-004.explanation: Power is proportional to V²f, so halving both V and f gives (1/2)² × 1/2 = 1/8. The computation takes twice as long, so energy is 1/8 × 2 = 1/4. Equivalently, since energy per switching event is proportional to CV², energy scales with the square of voltage. In practice the voltage range is limited and static power exists, so the reduction is not this ideal.
choiceNotes: Correct. Power scales with V²f and energy with V².
Voltage is also lowered, so the reduction is larger.
Lowering voltage also reduces energy.

power-management-005.question: Which describes static (leakage) power in CMOS circuits?
choices: Power that grows in proportion to clock speed
Power consumed continuously by leakage currents through off transistors and the like, even when signals do not switch
Power used only when manufacturing the chip
power-management-005.explanation: Transistors are not perfect switches; even when off, small subthreshold and gate leakage currents flow. Each is tiny, but across billions of transistors they add up to significant power, which grew more prominent as scaling lowered threshold voltages. Static power does not fall when clocks stop, so it is addressed by cutting supply power itself, for example with power gating.
choiceNotes: Power proportional to frequency is dynamic power.
Correct. It flows even with the clock stopped.
It is consumed during operation.

power-management-006.question: How does leakage power change as chip temperature rises, and what problem can result?
choices: It rises steeply (exponentially) with temperature, possibly causing a vicious cycle of more heat and higher temperature (thermal runaway)
It falls as temperature rises, so hotter means more efficient
It is constant regardless of temperature
power-management-006.explanation: Subthreshold leakage rises steeply with temperature because the energy distribution of carriers broadens, and it can increase substantially with roughly every 10°C. More leakage means more heat, higher temperature and still more leakage, a positive feedback loop that can lead to thermal runaway if cooling is insufficient. Temperature sensors therefore monitor the chip and controls such as lowering frequency are applied.
choiceNotes: Correct. Cooling design must account for it.
It increases instead.
It depends strongly on temperature.

power-management-007.question: Which describes power gating?
choices: Stopping only the clock supply to circuit blocks
Switching off the power supply to unused circuit blocks, eliminating nearly all their leakage power too
Doubling the supply voltage to speed up processing
power-management-007.explanation: Clock gating stops switching and so cuts dynamic power, but leakage continues as long as power is connected. Power gating turns off a large transistor switch placed between the block and the supply, cutting power itself, so leakage nearly disappears too. Smartphone SoCs aggressively power off idle CPU cores, GPUs and accelerators.
choiceNotes: That is clock gating.
Correct. Its key feature is cutting static power too.
It is a power-saving technique.

power-management-008.question: Which correctly pairs a caveat of power-gated blocks with its countermeasure?
choices: Contents always survive power-off, so nothing is needed
Flip-flop contents are lost, so needed state is saved in retention registers or external memory before power-off
Power-off doubles the voltage of other blocks
power-management-008.explanation: Flip-flops and SRAM in a powered-off block lose their contents, so to resume where it left off, state must be saved before cutting power. Options include retention registers, which pair each flip-flop with a small always-powered storage element, or software writing state out to memory. Saving, restoring and powering up cost time and energy, so for short idle periods it may be better not to cut power.
choiceNotes: Ordinary flip-flops lose their contents when unpowered.
Correct. Wake-up time and energy must also be considered.
Other blocks' voltages do not change.

power-management-009.question: Which correctly compares clock gating and power gating?
choices: Both have exactly the same effect and overhead
Clock gating cuts dynamic power and resumes instantly; power gating also cuts leakage but takes time to resume
Power gating reduces only dynamic power
power-management-009.explanation: Clock gating only stops the clock, so state is retained and operation resumes on the next clock, but leakage continues. Power gating cuts power and so also eliminates leakage, but needs time to save and restore state and for the supply to stabilize. They are combined: clock gating for idle periods of a few cycles, power gating for long ones.
choiceNotes: Their effects and overheads differ.
Correct. The choice depends on how long the idle period is.
Power gating also cuts leakage.

power-management-010.question: In power gating, why are a block's power switches often turned on gradually in sequence rather than all at once?
choices: To avoid a large inrush current charging the block's capacitance all at once, which would sag the supply and make other running circuits malfunction
Turning all switches on at once doubles the block's contents
Switches can only be fabricated one at a time
power-management-010.explanation: A powered-off block has large wiring and transistor capacitance, and a large current flows to charge it the instant power is connected. Turning on every switch at once can momentarily drop the supply network voltage sharply, risking malfunction in other blocks sharing it. So power-up follows a sequence, such as charging gradually through small switches before turning on the large ones.
choiceNotes: Correct. It limits supply noise.
Contents do not multiply.
It is unrelated to fabrication.

power-management-011.question: What is the role of the isolation cells placed between a powered-off block and running blocks?
choices: To pass a fixed value (0 or 1) to the running side even when the powered-off block's outputs become undefined
To convert supply voltages between the two blocks
To cool the powered-off block
power-management-011.explanation: Outputs of a powered-off block float at undefined intermediate voltages, which could make receiving circuits malfunction or draw shoot-through current in their input stages. Isolation cells clamp those outputs to fixed values while the block is off. Which signals are clamped to which values is conveyed to design tools in a file describing the power intent.
choiceNotes: Correct. It keeps undefined values from spreading.
Voltage conversion is the level shifter's job.
It has nothing to do with temperature.

power-management-012.question: What is the role of a level shifter inserted when passing signals between two blocks running at different supply voltages?
choices: To double the signal frequency
To encrypt the signal
To convert the signal's voltage to 0 and 1 levels matching the receiving side's supply
power-management-012.explanation: If a block running at 0.6 V sends a 1 (0.6 V) to a block running at 1.0 V, the receiver sees an intermediate voltage it cannot reliably read as 1, causing malfunction or shoot-through current. A level shifter converts the signal to voltages suited to the receiving side's supply. Designs that save power by running blocks at different voltages need them on every signal crossing a voltage boundary.
choiceNotes: It does not change frequency.
It does not encrypt.
Correct. It is especially needed going from low to high voltage.

power-management-013.question: What is the main purpose of dividing an SoC into multiple power domains?
choices: To cut total power by setting each block's voltage to its performance needs and powering off only idle blocks
To ensure all blocks always run at the same voltage
To shrink the chip area
power-management-013.explanation: CPU cores, the GPU, memory controllers and small always-on management circuits differ in the performance they need and in when they run. Separate power domains let only the blocks that need speed run at high voltage, idle blocks be powered off and only essential circuits stay powered during standby. Boundaries need level shifters and isolation cells, making design and verification more complex.
choiceNotes: Correct. Power can be managed at a fine grain.
With one voltage there would be no need to split.
The extra circuitry actually increases area.

power-management-014.question: What is the break-even time used to decide whether powering off an idle block pays off?
choices: The years needed to recoup a chip's purchase price through electricity savings
The idle duration needed for the energy saved by powering off to exceed the energy spent saving and restoring state and powering up
The time from power-on until the chip fails
power-management-014.explanation: Powering off reduces leakage, but saving and restoring state, recharging supply capacitance and restarting clocks cost fixed energy and time. For short idle periods, this overhead exceeds the energy saved, making it a net loss. OSes and power-management circuits predict idle durations and enter deep power-saving states only when the idle time is expected to exceed the break-even time.
choiceNotes: It is not about financial payback.
Correct. If the idle period is shorter, it is better not to power off.
It is not about lifetime.

power-management-015.question: Which describes CPU C-states?
choices: Combinations of frequency and voltage while the CPU is running
States representing how deeply an idle CPU sleeps; deeper states use less power but take longer to wake
Names of CPU manufacturing steps
power-management-015.explanation: Among C-states, C0 is executing instructions, C1 is a shallow sleep that merely stops the clock, and deeper states flush caches and power off the core, stopping more circuitry as the number grows. Deeper states save more power but take longer and cost more to exit, so the OS predicts the time until the next work and chooses an appropriate depth.
choiceNotes: That is a P-state.
Correct. C0 is active; larger numbers mean deeper sleep.
It is not a manufacturing step.

power-management-016.question: Which describes CPU P-states?
choices: Performance levels while the CPU runs, defined by combinations of frequency and voltage
How deeply the CPU sleeps when idle
Types of CPU package
power-management-016.explanation: P-states divide a running CPU's frequency and voltage combinations into levels; higher levels are faster and use more power. The OS or the CPU's internal power-management circuitry switches P-states to match load (DVFS). Combined with C-states, which describe sleep depth, this lets the CPU run at a suitable speed when there is work and sleep deeply when there is none.
choiceNotes: Correct. They correspond to DVFS levels.
That is a C-state.
It is not a package type.

power-management-017.question: When does "race to idle" (finishing work fast and then sleeping deeply) tend to save energy?
choices: When there is only dynamic power and no static power at all
When static power and the power of other components, such as memory, that stay active during work are large, so sleeping sooner shuts them all down
When entering sleep does not reduce power at all
power-management-017.explanation: Considering dynamic power alone, computing slowly at low voltage uses less energy. In reality, leakage and the power of memory, peripherals, the display and so on continue while the system is active. When these are large, finishing quickly at high performance and entering deep sleep, shutting everything down, uses less total energy. Which strategy wins depends on each device's power breakdown.
choiceNotes: Then running slowly at low voltage is better.
Correct. Shortening active time pays off more.
If sleep saves nothing, sleeping early is pointless.

power-management-018.question: What is the role of a governor, such as a cpufreq governor, that sets CPU frequency in Linux and other OSes?
choices: To set the frequency at which CPUs are manufactured
To change the color of the CPU cooling fan
To choose frequency and voltage levels matching required performance, based on load such as CPU utilization
power-management-018.explanation: A governor is a software policy that checks CPU load at intervals and selects operating levels, raising frequency when busy and lowering it when there is headroom. Policies include always maximum performance, always power saving and load-dependent scaling. On recent CPUs, hardware increasingly fine-tunes frequency itself, with the OS merely indicating whether to favor performance or efficiency.
choiceNotes: It has nothing to do with manufacturing.
It has nothing to do with fan color.
Correct. Software balances performance and power.

power-management-019.question: Which describes CPU turbo operation (such as Turbo Boost)?
choices: Automatically raising frequency above the rated value to boost performance when power and temperature allow
Always running at minimum frequency to save power
Attaching a tiny jet engine to the CPU
power-management-019.explanation: A CPU's rated frequency is set so that power and thermal limits hold even with every core heavily loaded. In practice there is headroom when only some cores are busy or the chip is cool. Turbo operation monitors power, temperature and current and raises frequency and voltage to use that headroom for more performance, automatically backing off when it runs out.
choiceNotes: Correct. It converts headroom into performance.
That is power-saving operation.
Of course no engine is attached.

power-management-020.question: Which describes thermal throttling?
choices: Stopping the fan to cool the chip
Raising chip temperature to speed up processing
Lowering frequency and voltage when the chip gets too hot, reducing heat to protect it from damage
power-management-020.explanation: When on-chip temperature sensors exceed a set threshold, the power-management circuitry or OS lowers frequency and voltage to bring heat within the cooling capacity. Performance drops, but chip failure and shortened lifetime are prevented. Thin laptops and smartphones slow down partway through sustained heavy work because of this throttling. If temperature keeps rising anyway, the system finally shuts down for protection.
choiceNotes: Stopping the fan would make it hotter.
Higher temperature does not speed things up.
Correct. It trades performance for safety.

power-management-021.question: Some CPU power limits let the chip run above the long-term average limit (close to TDP) for short periods. Why does this work?
choices: Chips and coolers have heat capacity, so temperature does not rise instantly and limits can be respected under brief high power
Using power briefly produces no heat
TDP indicates a minimum, not an upper limit
power-management-021.explanation: Heat goes into raising the temperature of the die, heat spreader and heat sink, and reaching steady-state temperature takes seconds to tens of seconds. So for short periods, power above the cooling capacity can be used without hitting the temperature limit. CPUs have a long-term average power limit and a higher short-term limit, speeding up brief tasks such as responding to user input. If the load persists, power falls back to the long-term limit.
choiceNotes: Correct. It exploits the thermal time constant.
Power always becomes heat.
TDP is a guideline for cooling design.

power-management-022.question: What is the most suitable use of features such as Intel RAPL that let software measure CPU and memory power and set caps?
choices: Finding CPU manufacturing defects
In data centers, capping each server's power so rack or building power limits are not exceeded
Finding grammar errors in programs
power-management-022.explanation: In data centers, power supply and cooling capacity cap the available power. If software can measure CPU and memory power and set limits, more servers can be installed while respecting the cap, without provisioning for the worst case of every server drawing maximum power. Measuring how much energy a program uses also helps guide energy-saving improvements.
choiceNotes: It is not a manufacturing test function.
Correct. Power becomes a manageable resource.
It is not a syntax checker.

power-management-023.question: Which describes ACPI, used in PCs and similar systems?
choices: The name of a CPU instruction set
A standard interface between hardware and OS that lets the OS manage device power states, power saving and thermals
A wireless LAN standard
power-management-023.explanation: ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface) is the standard mechanism by which an OS manages system and device power states. Firmware describes the hardware configuration and how to control power to the OS in tables, which the OS uses to enter sleep (S3) or hibernation (S4), control CPU C-states and P-states, drive fans according to temperature and so on. It also hides hardware-specific differences from the OS.
choiceNotes: It is not an instruction set.
Correct. It also controls sleep and hibernation.
It is not a wireless LAN standard.

power-management-024.question: In smartphone SoCs combining high-performance and efficient cores, why does running light work on the efficient cores use less energy?
choices: Efficient cores execute no instructions
Efficient cores are smaller and simpler and can run at lower voltage, so energy per instruction is lower
Efficient cores run on an external battery
power-management-024.explanation: High-performance cores exercise much circuitry per instruction through out-of-order execution, large caches and so on, so they are fast but use more energy per instruction. Efficient cores are smaller and simpler, with less switched capacitance, and can run at lower voltage. Light work such as checking notifications or playing music is well served by efficient cores, so the OS scheduler assigns work according to its weight.
choiceNotes: They do execute instructions.
Correct. Its performance is enough for light work.
They run on the same battery.

power-management-025.question: Which describes the idea behind adaptive voltage scaling (AVS)?
choices: Running every chip at a high voltage set for the slowest chip
Changing voltage randomly every time
Measuring each chip's speed and temperature on chip and approaching the minimum voltage at which it works, trimming wasted voltage margin
power-management-025.explanation: Manufacturing variation makes some chips of the same product fast and others slow. Running every chip at a voltage that works even for the slowest wastes power on fast chips, whose voltage is higher than necessary. With AVS, on-chip ring oscillators or delay-measuring circuits check actual speed, and voltage is adjusted to just what that chip needs, accounting for temperature and aging.
choiceNotes: That is the traditional, margin-heavy approach.
Voltage is not changed randomly.
Correct. It exploits chip-to-chip variation.

power-management-026.question: Which is NOT a reason chips need margin in their supply voltage?
choices: When circuits switch together, supply wiring resistance and inductance cause momentary voltage drops (supply noise)
Higher voltage always reduces power consumption
Manufacturing variation, temperature and aging change circuit speed
power-management-026.explanation: Circuits slow down with even a slight voltage drop and can miss timing. When many circuits switch at once, resistive drop in the supply wiring (IR drop) and inductive voltage from rapid current changes momentarily lower the voltage. Speed also varies with process, temperature and aging, so some margin is needed. But margin also wastes power, so it is reduced through stronger power delivery networks, AVS and similar techniques.
choiceNotes: This is a reason margin is needed.
Correct. Raising voltage increases power.
This is a reason margin is needed.

power-management-027.question: What is an advantage of placing the regulators that generate CPU supply voltages inside the chip or package rather than on the motherboard (integrated regulators)?
choices: Chip heat always disappears
The chip can run without any supply voltage
Voltage can be set per core and switched faster, enabling finer-grained, quicker DVFS
power-management-027.explanation: Motherboard regulators are distant and work through large capacitive components, so voltage changes are slow and providing many separate rails is difficult. Regulators inside the chip or package can generate separate voltages per core and switch in a microsecond or less, enabling power saving that tracks load changes quickly. On the other hand, the regulators' loss heat and area are added to the chip side.
choiceNotes: The regulators' own losses add heat inside the chip.
A supply voltage is still needed.
Correct. In exchange, on-chip heat and area increase.

power-management-028.question: Why is the energy-delay product (EDP) sometimes preferred over energy alone in evaluating low-power designs?
choices: Energy alone can favor designs made extremely slow to save energy, so EDP evaluates the balance with speed
EDP is simpler to compute than energy
Using EDP always makes power zero
power-management-028.explanation: Lowering voltage and frequency drastically shrinks energy per computation but makes processing impractically slow. The energy-delay product multiplies energy per operation by the time it takes, so cutting energy at the cost of a large slowdown does not improve the score, allowing designs to be compared on the balance of performance and efficiency. When speed matters even more, a metric multiplying by the square of time is used.
choiceNotes: Correct. Smaller is better for both energy and time.
It adds a multiplication; it is not simpler.
Changing the metric does not change power.

power-management-029.question: What is the closest efficiency of a linear regulator (LDO) producing 1.0 V from a 1.8 V input (ignoring the regulator's own quiescent current)?
choices: About 80%
About 95%
About 56%
power-management-029.explanation: A linear regulator passes the same current at input and output and maintains the output voltage by dissipating the voltage difference as heat in a transistor. Efficiency is therefore roughly output voltage ÷ input voltage: 1.0 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 56%, with the remaining 44% turned into heat. It suits small input-output differences or noise-sensitive loads; for large differences, a switching regulator usually steps the voltage down first.
choiceNotes: In a linear regulator the entire voltage difference is lost.
Such efficiency requires a switching regulator.

power-management-030.question: A device drawing 300 mA on average runs from a 3000 mAh battery. Roughly how many hours does it run (ignoring voltage drop and similar)?
choices: About 1 hour
About 100 hours
About 10 hours
power-management-030.explanation: mAh (milliampere-hours) is a battery capacity unit indicating how many milliamps can flow for how many hours. Drawing an average of 300 mA from a 3000 mAh battery depletes it in 3000 ÷ 300 = 10 hours. Halving the average current doubles the runtime. In practice, battery voltage changes, temperature and reduced efficiency at high current make this an estimate.
choiceNotes: The order of magnitude is wrong.
The order of magnitude is wrong.

power-management-031.question: What is the difference between power and energy?
choices: Power and energy are the same thing with the same unit
Energy is a unit of voltage and power a unit of current
Power is energy used per unit time (W), and energy is power accumulated over time (J)
power-management-031.explanation: Power (watts) is the rate of use at a given moment and matters for heat and supply design. Energy (joules) is power times time and matters for battery life and electricity bills. Halving power while doubling time leaves energy unchanged. When considering power-saving measures, it is important to distinguish whether the issue is temperature (power) or battery life (energy).
choiceNotes: They are different quantities.
Voltage is in V, current in A.
Correct. Running at 1 W for 1 second uses 1 J.

power-management-032.question: Which metric is most suitable for comparing processor energy efficiency?
choices: Clock frequency alone
Performance per watt (performance ÷ power)
Chip weight
power-management-032.explanation: Performance divided by power (for example, operations per second per watt) shows how much work one joule of energy accomplishes, and it matters both for battery-powered devices and for data centers burdened by electricity and cooling costs. High frequency with little work per clock or high power still means poor efficiency. Comparisons should measure the same work under the same conditions.
choiceNotes: Frequency alone says nothing about power or work per clock.
Correct. It shows how much work is done for the same power.
Weight is irrelevant.

power-management-033.question: In today's chips, which statement comparing the energy of moving data and computing is generally correct?
choices: Reading data from external DRAM costs tens to hundreds of times the energy of one operation, so reusing data locally saves energy
Moving data costs no energy; only computation does
One operation costs hundreds of times more energy than a DRAM read
power-management-033.explanation: Compared with computation over short wires inside an arithmetic unit, moving data off chip to DRAM through long wires and pins costs far more energy. Even on chip, nearby registers cost less energy than distant caches. So keeping data in nearby storage for reuse, reducing data volume (with lower precision) and computing near the data are major ways to save energy.
choiceNotes: Correct. Caches and locality help power too.
Data movement consumes a lot of energy.
It is the other way around.

power-management-034.question: Among DRAM power-saving states, which describes self-refresh?
choices: A low-power state in which the DRAM keeps refreshing itself to retain its contents even with no commands from the memory controller
A state that erases all DRAM contents
A state that doubles DRAM frequency
power-management-034.explanation: DRAM loses its contents without periodic refresh, normally commanded by the memory controller. In self-refresh, the DRAM keeps refreshing itself with an internal oscillator, so contents survive even with the memory controller and interface circuits shut down. It is used while PCs and smartphones sleep, allowing work to resume immediately on wake.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is used during system sleep and similar.
Contents are retained.
It does not raise frequency.

power-management-035.question: DRAM operated at high temperature may require shorter refresh intervals. Which pairs the reason with the effect on power correctly?
choices: At high temperature cell charge increases, so refreshes and power decrease
Temperature and refresh interval are unrelated
At high temperature cell leakage rises and charge is lost faster, so refreshes increase and so does power
power-management-035.explanation: DRAM cells hold information as charge on capacitors, and rising temperature increases leakage so charge drains faster. To avoid losing data, refresh must occur more often, and many standards halve the refresh interval in the high-temperature range. Refresh power rises accordingly, and so does the time the DRAM is unavailable during refresh, so cooling also affects DRAM power and performance.
choiceNotes: Charge is lost faster, not gained.
It depends strongly on temperature.
Correct. Standards commonly double the refresh rate above 85°C.

power-management-036.question: To cut power on a microcontroller, what should be done with unused peripherals such as timers and UARTs?
choices: Stop the clock supply to those peripherals through configuration registers
Keep those peripherals running at maximum speed
Set all their pins to output 1
power-management-036.explanation: On many microcontrollers, peripheral clocks may be off or on after reset, so firmware configures clocks only for the peripherals in use. With its clock stopped, a peripheral consumes no dynamic switching power. Also, leaving unused pins floating can cause shoot-through current in input circuits, so defining their states reduces power further.
choiceNotes: Correct. Most microcontrollers can gate clocks per peripheral.
Running unused circuits wastes power.
Pin settings must consider what is connected.

power-management-037.question: What is the role of a PMIC (power management IC) used in smartphones and similar devices?
choices: Generating the multiple voltages the SoC, memory and peripherals need from the battery and managing power-up sequencing and voltage changes
Generating images for the display
Transmitting and receiving radio signals
power-management-037.explanation: SoC cores, memory, I/O, cameras and sensors each need different voltages. A PMIC integrates many switching regulators and LDOs, efficiently generating the required voltages from the battery and, as directed by the SoC, changing voltages for DVFS, switching power to blocks on and off and powering up in the required order. Some also manage battery charging and fuel gauging.
choiceNotes: Correct. Some also manage battery charging.
Images come from the GPU and similar.
Radio is handled by RF components.

power-management-038.question: In chips using multiple supply voltages, why must the power-up order (power sequencing) be observed?
choices: A wrong order can drive signals into unpowered circuits or push large currents through protection devices, causing malfunction, latch-up or damage
Following the order makes the chip run twice as fast
The order is cosmetic and does not affect operation
power-management-038.explanation: For example, if the I/O supply comes up before the core supply, current can flow from the I/O side into the unpowered core, or circuits in an undefined state may drive signals externally. Large currents through protection diodes can trigger latch-up or damage. So chip datasheets specify the order for powering up and down, and PMICs or similar control the supplies accordingly.
choiceNotes: Correct. The order specified in the datasheet must be followed.
It has nothing to do with speed.
It affects operation and reliability.

power-management-039.question: What characterizes near-threshold operation, running with supply voltage lowered close to the transistor threshold?
choices: Speed rises and energy falls
Lowering voltage does not change power
It greatly reduces energy per operation, but speed falls sharply and variation has a much larger effect
power-management-039.explanation: Energy per switching event is proportional to CV², so lowering voltage close to threshold cuts energy to a fraction. But transistor current shrinks, so circuits slow dramatically, and even small threshold variations change speed greatly. It is being researched and used for devices such as sensor nodes, where modest speed suffices and long battery life is the goal.
choiceNotes: Lower voltage makes circuits slower.
Lower voltage reduces power substantially.
Correct. It suits uses where battery life matters more than speed.

power-management-040.question: As supply voltage is lowered, total energy per operation reaches a minimum at some voltage and then rises if voltage is lowered further. Why?
choices: Below that point circuits become so slow that leakage energy accumulated during each operation grows faster than dynamic energy shrinks
Lowering voltage increases dynamic energy
Lowering voltage increases the number of transistors
power-management-040.explanation: Dynamic energy falls with the square of voltage. Leakage energy, however, is leakage power times the time per operation, and as voltage drops circuits slow and that time grows rapidly, so leakage energy rises sharply below some voltage. The voltage minimizing their sum is the minimum energy point, often near or slightly below the threshold voltage.
choiceNotes: Correct. That minimum is called the minimum energy point.
Dynamic energy falls as voltage drops.
The transistor count does not change.

power-management-041.question: A 50 W CPU is fitted with a cooler of thermal resistance 0.5 K/W. Roughly how many degrees above ambient does the chip run (ignoring other heat paths)?
choices: About 100°C
About 25°C
About 0.01°C
power-management-041.explanation: Thermal resistance is the temperature rise per watt of heat flow, so temperature rise = power × thermal resistance. 50 W × 0.5 K/W = 25 K, so with 25°C ambient the chip sits around 50°C. Doubling power doubles the rise, so working backward from the allowed temperature determines the usable power limit or the cooler performance required.
choiceNotes: Multiply by the thermal resistance; do not divide.
That divides by the thermal resistance.

power-management-042.question: Why are temperature sensors often placed at many locations within a large chip?
choices: More sensors cool the chip
Temperature sensors can be used only once
Areas such as dense arithmetic units heat up locally (hot spots), so a single sensor cannot reveal the hottest point
power-management-042.explanation: Power usage varies greatly across a chip, and active cores or arithmetic units can run tens of degrees hotter than cache regions. Temperature limits are set by the hottest spot, so a single sensor might miss a hot spot reaching a dangerous temperature. Sensors are placed at many locations, and frequency control or throttling is based on the highest reading.
choiceNotes: Sensors do not cool anything.
Sensors work repeatedly.
Correct. Control is based on the hottest spot.

power-management-043.question: In data centers packed with high-performance AI GPUs, why is liquid cooling spreading alongside air cooling?
choices: Liquid cooling doubles a chip's performance limit
Air cooling has been banned by law
Power per chip and per rack has grown so high that air can no longer carry the heat away adequately
power-management-043.explanation: A single AI GPU consumes several hundred watts to over 1 kW, and racks full of them produce tens of kilowatts to over 100 kW of heat. Air carries little heat per volume, so even stronger fans can no longer keep up. Liquids such as water carry thousands of times more heat per volume, so cold plates on chips with circulating liquid are coming into use. It also reduces the power spent on cooling.
choiceNotes: The performance limit itself does not double.
It has not been banned.
Correct. Liquids carry far more heat than air.

power-management-044.question: Which describes PUE, a metric of data center power efficiency?
choices: Performance per CPU; larger is better
A measure of data center floor area
Total facility power divided by IT equipment power; the closer to 1, the less is wasted on cooling and the like
power-management-044.explanation: PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) is total data center power divided by the power used by servers, storage and network equipment. It grows with power spent on cooling, power conversion losses, lighting and so on. A PUE of 1.5, for example, means half of the IT power again goes to cooling and overhead. Some facilities achieve about 1.1 with efficient cooling using outside air or liquid.
choiceNotes: It is not a performance metric.
It is not an area metric.
Correct. The ideal is 1.0.

power-management-045.question: Why do smartphone SoCs play video using dedicated video decoder circuits rather than the general-purpose CPU?
choices: CPUs cannot play video
Dedicated circuits automatically improve image quality
Circuits specialized for a task use far less energy than doing it on the CPU, extending battery life
power-management-045.explanation: A general-purpose CPU, designed to handle anything, spends much energy beyond the computation itself on fetching and decoding instructions and reading and writing registers. A dedicated circuit such as a video decoder hard-wires a fixed processing flow, doing the same work with a fraction, even a few percent, of the energy. SoCs carry many dedicated blocks for video, images, audio, AI and more.
choiceNotes: CPUs can play video but use more power.
It is not for improving image quality.
Correct. Specialization greatly improves energy efficiency.

power-management-046.question: Why does an OS slightly shift and align the wake-up times of many programs' timers (timer coalescing)?
choices: To improve timer accuracy
To reduce the number of programs
To reduce how often the CPU wakes and lengthen each idle period, making deep power-saving states easier to enter
power-management-046.explanation: If many programs set timers at scattered times, the CPU must wake for each, idle periods stay short and deep power-saving states are out of reach. The OS groups timer expirations that can tolerate a little delay into nearby times and handles them together on one wake-up. Idle periods lengthen beyond the break-even time, allowing deep sleep and greatly reducing standby power.
choiceNotes: Accuracy actually drops slightly.
The number of programs does not change.
Correct. It accepts small delays to process work together.

power-management-047.question: What is the idea behind the tickless kernel used in Linux and other OSes?
choices: Hiding the clock display to reduce screen power
When idle, the periodic timer tick interrupt is stopped so the CPU can sleep until the next work
Raising the timer tick interrupt to tens of thousands per second
power-management-047.explanation: Traditional OSes used a timer tick interrupt, say 100 to 1000 times per second, for task switching and timekeeping, waking the CPU each time even with nothing to do. A tickless kernel stops the tick on idle CPUs and programs a timer only for the next time it actually needs to wake. The CPU can then sleep longer and deeper, reducing standby power.
choiceNotes: It has nothing to do with the display.
Correct. It reduces standby power.
It reduces interrupts instead.

power-management-048.question: What is the Arm WFI (Wait For Interrupt) instruction used for?
choices: Disabling all interrupts to speed up processing
Waiting for a Wi-Fi signal to arrive
Stopping the CPU in a low-power state while waiting for an interrupt when idle, resuming when one arrives
power-management-048.explanation: Waiting in an empty loop when idle keeps the CPU executing instructions and consuming power. Executing WFI puts the CPU into a low-power state, for example by stopping its clock, doing nothing until an interrupt arrives. It is used in OS idle loops and in microcontroller main loops waiting for the next interrupt. x86 has a similar HLT instruction.
choiceNotes: It does not disable interrupts.
It has nothing to do with Wi-Fi.
Correct. It saves far more power than spinning in an empty loop.

power-management-049.question: What is commonly used to wake a battery-powered device from sleep at a set time?
choices: Keeping the CPU running at maximum frequency
An alarm from a real-time clock (RTC) that keeps running on tiny power during sleep
Removing and reinserting the battery
power-management-049.explanation: Even during sleep, a small real-time clock driven by a 32.768 kHz crystal or similar keeps time on a microampere or less. At the set time it raises an alarm interrupt that wakes the CPU. Other wake sources include button or sensor signal changes and incoming communications. Configuring which sources may wake the device lets it sleep deeply the rest of the time.
choiceNotes: Then it is not sleeping at all.
Correct. Pin-change interrupts and the like can also wake it.
Removing the battery loses the time and other state.

power-management-050.question: If only the supply voltage is lowered by 10% (all else equal), by roughly what percentage does dynamic power fall?
choices: About 19%
About 10%
About 50%
power-management-050.explanation: Dynamic power is proportional to the square of voltage, so scaling voltage by 0.9 scales power by 0.9² = 0.81, a reduction of about 19%. Even small voltage changes have a large effect on power, making voltage reduction one of the most effective power-saving levers. Lower voltage slows circuits, though, so it must stay within the range that keeps required speed, and doing this according to load is what DVFS does.
choiceNotes: Correct. 0.9² = 0.81, about a 19% reduction.
Power is proportional to the square of voltage.
A 10% change does not cut it that much.
